abstract: Whole-plant water-transport capacity largely controls terrestrial water fluxes, yet it is unresolved to what extent its variation across the seed-plant phylogeny is structured by shared ancestry, edaphoclimatic conditions, plant height or water relation traits. We fitted a phylogenetic structural equation model to maximum leaf-specific whole-plant hydraulic conductance (kL), together with concurrent Huber value (Hv), stomatal conductance (gs), and height for 263 species spanning the global climate space, partitioning direct from indirect effects, and phylogenetically conserved from independent effects. kL declined with height, and Hv did not offset this decline. Hv raised kL but was unrelated to height among species. kL was lower in wetter niches, despite higher Hv there, indicating lower conductance per unit sapwood area. kL was tightly coupled to gs in both conserved and independent variation, so the height-driven decline in kL propagated to gas exchange. Plant height therefore constrains whole-plant hydraulic supply and, through it, gs.
